newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-RUSSELL BARTON'S CANBERRA CLOSEUP-TAX REFORM HOTS UP.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-RUSSELL BARTON'S CANBERRA CLOSEUP-TAX REFORM HOTS UP.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
In choking off A$5.0 billion of the states' revenue, the High Court could be seen to have thrown into question the very structure of our federation.
In other words, is there a future for the states?
The so-called business franchise licence fees, now invalid, represented around 15 percent of the states' revenue but, more importantly, a very big chunk of the revenue they raise themselves.
Before the judgement the states received 80 percent of their funds from the federal government, raising 20 percent directly. That split is now 83 to 17 percent.
The direct revenue sources left to the states comprise payroll tax -- acknowledged as an anti-employment measure -- stamp duty, and the new milch cow, gambling.
But the tobacco, alcohol and petrol imposts were growth taxes, the first two aided by the community's more ready acceptance of rises in these areas on health grounds.

(And the states' recent tendency to 'go for growth' with repeated hikes in the tobacco tax in particular, fuelled the High Court's adverse decision, the majority four to three judgement noting that the states had far overreached the levels of revenue which might have been regarded as reasonable under a fee to carry on business).

That's the background to the new pressure the states have begun to apply to the Howard government for the wholesale shake-up of the Commonwealth-State financial arrangements to restore certainty to the states' base.
The calls from state premiers range from ludicrous to reasonable.
Western Australia's Richard Court is demanding the federal government call a referendum to simply hand over much of the tax base to the states.
Others want a special premiers' conference to dicuss giving the states a fixed share of Commonwealth revenue, a pitch they've been making for years.
What it all means is that the time for fiddling at the edges of the tax structure is over.

All premiers also back reform to the indirect tax base -- New South Wales' Bob Carr got into trouble this week with his federal colleagues by indicating he could accept a goods and services tax (GST) as long as it had stringent safeguards.
That position didn't last long -- a spokesman rang around media outlets hours later to say the premier didn't support a GST after all, despite the words which came from his own lips.
Carefully handled, the states' call for an indirect tax shake-up -- meaning a GST -- is no bad thing for the federal government.
John Howard's whole approach to the tax issue has centred on trying to appear to be responding to pressure rather than striking out in the lead, as did Paul Keating and John Hewson to their cost.
There are now few vocal opponents to a broad-based indirect tax, with almost all major business groups taking part in a task force to apply that pressure.

The big difference this time is that the welfare lobby now is also accepting the inevitability of reform, by taking part in the task force, and other special studies such as today's CEDA-Brotherhood of St Laurence project to highlight the deficiencies of the current tax system.

A Treasury team is now working on possible policy changes. It is led by Dr Ken Henry who was senior economic adviser to Paul Keating during the preparation of the 1985 tax reform white paper and the tax summit.
The ground is pretty well-worn. For Howard and Costello, the task is to time the government's take-off on the private sector reform wave and surf it into the next election.

But they won't be getting any help from Labor. Despite Bob Carr's little gaffe -- very similar to Gareth Evans' words earlier this year which led to a public admonishment, Kim Beazley says Labor is irrevocably opposed to a GST.

Labor's gambing on electoral suppport at the risk of being completely isolated on the issue. Beazley says he's not opposed to reform to the wholesale sales tax, but when asked how it should be done without a GST he skirts the issue.
It's just possible therefore that Labor could be on the wrong horse this time. The High Court's decision has only intensified the pressure for change.
And the chaotic aftermath, perversely, could help Howard by helping to convince the electorate that change is necessary, tipping the anti-GST balance evident in John Hewson's 1993 loss the other way.
In this climate, Labor will have to be a lot more clever than to adopt a simple rejection of the GST, without a coherent alternative.
Prepare for yet another tax election in 1999.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
